tagline.text: A 19th-century stone ancestral house on the Iloilo River in Arevalo, now a museum and chocolate restaurant

location.label: Location
location.text: 20 Osmeña Street, Arevalo district, Iloilo City

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Year-round (the dry season, December–May, is easier for getting around)

children.text: Camiña Balay nga Bato is a 19th-century stone ancestral house on the riverbank in the Arevalo district of Iloilo City. The National Museum declared it an Important Cultural Property in 2015, and today it operates as a museum, gift shop and restaurant famous for handmade tsokolate and pancit molo.

Camiña Balay nga Bato stands at 20 Osmeña Street in the Arevalo (Villa de Arevalo) district, southwest of central Iloilo City. "Balay nga bato" means "stone house" in Hiligaynon, and the building is a bahay na bato, the style of house that upper-class families built in the Spanish colonial Philippines. It is said to have been built by Don Fernando Avanceña for his wife, Eulalia Abaja, and sources give the construction date variously as the 1850s, 1860 or 1865. It is said to have been designed and built by a Catholic priest, Father Anselmo Avanceña.

The house stands here because of the river. The Avanceña family traded hablon, a handwoven cloth, and the Iloilo River beside the house was the route for carrying textiles to neighboring towns. The Camiña family, who care for the house today, still run a hablon business, and near the entrance you can see looms strung with red and yellow thread. The current owners are Gerard and Luth Camiña, described as the fourth generation, and they opened the house to the public in 2010 as a museum and restaurant. On December 23, 2015, the National Museum declared it an Important Cultural Property under Resolution No. 23-2015 and Republic Act No. 10066, and a marker was unveiled on February 22, 2019.

In architectural terms, the house is a "mestizo" blend of the bahay kubo tradition of bamboo and nipa roofing with Spanish-style stone. Thick walls of limestone and river sand kept the ground floor cool, and it served as a storeroom (almacen) for grain and cloth. The living quarters upstairs rest on wooden posts, said to number twenty-four, some of them carved. The second floor keeps its narra floors, kamagong wood walls, capiz shell windows and a striking stamped-metal ceiling. Some accounts also describe it as the lowest rank of Iloilo stone house, a three-bay structure.

Travelers experience the house as both a museum and a meal. The usual format is a guided look around the house, then kinihad biscuits and thick chocolate drink, tsokolate de batirol, and, if you like, a lunch buffet to follow. This guide is for travelers who want to spend part of a day in Iloilo City experiencing how people used to live and eat in one stop. Package prices and hours change, so confirm the latest details by phone or social media before you go. We could not confirm an official price list, so the prices below are approximate, based on past visitor accounts.

blocks.title: Second-floor living space and metal ceiling

children.text: Up the stairs, the second floor opens onto wide wooden floors, antique furniture and family heirlooms. The most eye-catching feature is the stamped-metal ceiling, covered in patterns. Follow your guide through the bedroom, the main hall (sala mayor), the kitchen and the dining room in turn.

The staircase from the ground floor to the second floor is built steeply, at about 45 degrees. The explanation passed down is that it was meant to keep thieves from climbing up easily. Hold the handrail going up and coming down.

The second floor has the altar where the family prayed, with old saints and Santo Niño statues. It is a space that gives a glimpse of the faith life of a Filipino Catholic household. Ask your guide before taking photographs.

blocks.title: The ground-floor gift shop, Lola Rufina

children.text: The ground floor, once the almacen, is now a gift shop and display room for antiques. It sells chocolate-making batirol pots, Iloilo textiles, furniture and small items, and it holds a grand piano described as the oldest in Iloilo. Some antiques are expensive, so check the condition before you negotiate.
Near the entrance, looms strung with red and yellow thread show how hablon is woven. It is a family trade the Camiña family carries on themselves, so it is also a good place to buy finished pieces.

This thick hot chocolate is made from roasted, ground cacao tablea and is whisked into a froth in front of you in a heated cast-iron jug, then poured into a small cup. It is said to follow a recipe passed down for three generations, and you dip kinihad, a biscuit similar to biscocho, into it. It is rich and sweet, so one cup is enough.

In a casual dining space once known as the balcon comedor, the buffet is known to include pancit molo (Molo soup), ratotoy, embutido de Arevalo, binuog nga baboy (pork), chicken inasal, garlic bangus and pancit miki Bisaya. The lineup can change from day to day, and vegetarian options are limited. Reservations are recommended for the buffet and for groups.

In front of the house stands the National Museum's Important Cultural Property (ICP) marker. It is the sign that the building has been declared a specially protected cultural property in the Philippines, so it is worth a photo at the entrance.

Take a taxi or Grab from your hotel in the city to Camiña Balay nga Bato on Osmeña Street in Arevalo. Visitor accounts say the ride usually takes 15 to 20 minutes from downtown, but it varies with traffic.

Iloilo's stone heritage is scattered across different districts, so taking a taxi or Grab is the efficient way to get between them.
There are several direct flights a day from Manila's Ninoy Aquino International Airport to Iloilo International Airport (ILO), and the flight takes about
1 hour 10–20 minutes
. Airlines and schedules change by season, so check when you book.
The airport is in Cabatuan, so you reach the city by taxi, Grab or an airport shuttle. Check travel time and fares locally.

items.title: Taxi or Grab from the city

children.text: From the city center (Iloilo City proper) to 20 Osmeña Street in Arevalo, a taxi or Grab is the easiest way. Visitor accounts put it at about
15–20 minutes
from downtown, but it varies with traffic.
We could not confirm public transport routes in visitor accounts. If it is your first time, enter "20 Osmeña Street, Arevalo" in the app and show it to the driver as well.
The landline is listed as (033) 336-3858 and a mobile number as (0917) 305-5355, but numbers may change. Reserve the lunch buffet and group visits in advance.

The visit centers on the house, so you can come all year. In the December–May dry season Iloilo has many clear days, which makes it easy to combine with a walk through the Molo district. In the June–November rainy season showers are frequent, so it suits an indoor plan.

The city is crowded during Dinagyang at the end of January, so book lodging and transport early. The house has two floors with steep stairs, so it is more comfortable to visit in the morning or late afternoon than in the heat of midday.

Camiña Balay nga Bato is in Arevalo, a little way from the city center, so most people visit as a day trip from a city hotel or from a hotel near the business park. Iloilo City proper has many mid-range hotels and the Iloilo Business Park area has large hotels, so choose what suits your plans. Hotel names and rates change a lot by season, so check recent reviews on a booking site.

What you must taste here are the tsokolate de batirol and the pancit molo. Pancit molo is a clear soup with dumplings made from wrappers, and is the signature dish of Iloilo's Molo district. The buffet also features local dishes such as ratotoy, embutido de Arevalo, pancit miki Bisaya and binuog nga baboy. Vegetarian choices are limited, so it is best to ask ahead.

Reservations are recommended for the lunch buffet and for group visits. Casual dress is fine.
The stairs to the second floor are steep and the floors are old, so wear low-heeled shoes and hold the handrail.
Ask your guide first whether you may photograph in the oratorio and in front of heirlooms, and do not touch furniture or relics.
The tsokolate is rich and one cup is enough, so if you do not like sweet drinks, choose a pancit molo package.
Hablon textiles and chocolate sticks make light souvenirs, but antique furniture is expensive, so check the price before you buy.
In a taxi, check whether the meter is used, and for Grab, enter the address in the app accurately.
When combining it with sights such as Jaro Cathedral and Molo Church on the same day, allow plenty of travel time.
The package prices in this guide come from a 2014 visitor account and are out of date. Be sure to confirm current prices and hours before you go.
This is a privately owned ancestral house, so opening hours and the way tours are run may change. Reserving is safest for groups or the buffet.
The construction date (the 1850s, 1860 or 1865) differs between sources, so this guide gives a range. Do not plan around an exact year.
The stairs are steep and the floors are old, so children and anyone with limited mobility should hold the handrail and move slowly.
Vegetarian options are limited, so mention any dietary restrictions when you reserve.
If a taxi driver refuses the meter and demands a flat fare, take another taxi.

This old mansion in the Molo district,
Molo Mansion
, gives you another glimpse of the lives of Iloilo's upper class when seen as a follow-up.
This leading church beside Jaro Plaza,
Jaro Cathedral

This riverside promenade, the
Iloilo River Esplanade
, is pleasant to walk around sunset. Seeing it after the house helps you understand why the house was built beside the river.
